# RBE 549, Lab 8 Report

Tom Kazakov

*Lab summary: calibrate a camera from checkerboard images, undistort, and evaluate the pipeline by applying known distortion and recovering the parameters. Analyze sample images from the OpenCV tutorial and bespoke calibration pattern images taken for the lab.*

# Part 1: OpenCV Samples

**![][image1]**   
*Figure 1\. OpenCV Samples processed with **cv**.drawChessboardCorners()*

1. The OpenCV sample set provided in the GitHub repo is missing image \#10 for the reason I was not able to establish, so there were 13 samples analyzed, not 14, as the name of the last one (“left14.jpg”) would imply.  
2. The board in the sample set has 10×7 squares, giving 9x6 inner corners. The tutorial code uses (7,6), which is a subset of the full pattern: 4 of 13 images fail detection at steep angles because the smaller sub-pattern can't be reliably located. Using the correct (9,6) gets 13/13.  
   ![][image2]  
   *Figure 2\. OpenCV subset with 7x6 corners query: four images don’t have corners recognized*  
3. Notably, the order of corner detection and the auto-assignment of the rainbow gradient differ depending on whether the request is for (9,6) or (7,6) corners.  
4. **calibrateCamera** solves a global optimization across all images at once. A single image of a known planar pattern gives a homography: enough for some constraints but not all. Multiple views from different angles over-determine the system, letting the solver recover all intrinsic parameters and distortion coefficients simultaneously. More images from diverse angles means a better-conditioned system; a single view would be underdetermined for all 5 distortion coefficients plus the intrinsic matrix.  
5. Calibration result: fx and fy both around 536 (which is expected for a camera with square sensor pixels), principal point near image center, k1 \= \-0.27 (barrel distortion), RMS reprojection error 0.41px, per-image error mean 0.041px.  
6. The script saves three .npy files, the format prescribed by the assignment. Alternatively, the arrays could have been zipped into a single .npz or pickled.   
7. After applying the correction, the slight barrel distortion visible in the images is rectified, as shown in Figure 3\. 

*![][image3]*  
*Figure 3\. Side-by-side comparison of OpenCV sample images after distortion correction has been applied. Most images had per-image error under 0.03px. Image 2 was an outlier at 0.17px; likely a steeper angle or slight motion blur degrading corner localization.*

# Part 2: Samples from BRIO, Distortion Recovery

1. Checkerboard calibration pattern produced with the geometry close to that used in OpenCV samples. The pattern was glued to a 3mm thick acrylic sheet for flatness.   
2. 18 checkerboard images from the Logitech BRIO at 3840x2160. All 18 pass corner detection.  
3. Baseline calibration: fx \~2264, fy \~2271, RMS 1.07px, mean error 0.14px.   
4. I noticed that the reprojection error is substantially higher in absolute terms than the one measured for OpenCV samples. This is likely caused by the resolution that is 6x higher. Normalized to the image resolution, it’s 0.000061 (BRIO) vs 0.000076 (OpenCV samples).  
5. While it’s likely that BRIO applies distortion correction in firmware before exposing the video stream via UVC, some residual distortion remains in the image. The residual distortion is most visible in Figure 4, where the pattern occupies most of the FoV and extends to the edges. k1 measured around 0.20.  
   ![][image4]  
   *Figure 4\. Pattern captured from above, barrel distortion is easily noticeable*   
6. Per-image errors ranged from 0.05 to 0.23px. Images 1 and 14 were the highest at 0.22 and 0.23px, respectively, both with the board at steep angles where perspective foreshortening compresses one side.  
7. To create images with artificial distortion, I applied a set of parameters that produce a pincushion effect as a visual experiment, since both the baseline distortion on the BRIO images and the OpenCV samples have a barrel effect: **k1=0.5, k2=-0.1, p1=0.01, p2=-0.005, k3=0.0**.   
8. 3 of 18 images lost corner detection after distortion: pincushion pushed corners near the frame edges out of view.  
9. Calibrating the distorted images recovers the total distortion the solver sees: the camera's baseline plus what I applied. Comparing against GT alone would ignore the baseline, making the recovery look worse than it is. The correct target is baseline \+ GT. The sum is a linear approximation of a nonlinear composition, but it holds well for the dominant terms.

| Param | Baseline | GT | Expected | Recovered | Delta |
| :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: |
| k1 | 0.195 | 0.500 | 0.695 | 0.702 | \+0.007 |
| k2 | \-0.500 | \-0.100 | \-0.600 | \-0.511 | \+0.089 |
| p1 | 0.001 | 0.010 | 0.011 | 0.012 | \+0.001 |
| p2 | 0.000 | \-0.005 | \-0.005 | \-0.002 | \+0.003 |
| k3 | 0.309 | 0.000 | 0.309 | 0.129 | \-0.180 |

   *Table 1\. Baseline \+ GT vs. Recovered (values rounded to three decimals)*

10. Overall, recovery from the distortion is in an acceptable range, as shown in Figure 5\.   
11. **getOptimalNewCameraMatrix** has an alpha parameter that controls what happens at the edges after correction. alpha=1 keeps all pixels but can stretch the image non-uniformly. I saw a visible horizontal stretch on the checkerboard squares because the new camera matrix adjusts fx and fy differently to fit everything. alpha=0 crops to valid pixels and produces clean output, but discards the periphery.

# Gen AI Usage

1. Claude Opus 4.6 for general conversational ideation, probing around assignment requirements, formulating approach & strategy. Doesn’t produce code. Does proofread my technical writing.   
2. For general code-writing, PyCharm with LLM-powered contextual suggestions, boilerplate writing, spellchecker, and linter.   
3. Claude Code in PyCharm for interactive code gen and refactoring; used Opus 4.6. All code produced by Gen AI for this assignment was reviewed and verified, and also refactored or recomposed to varying degrees. Commit history in the repo can serve as proof of organic authorship: [https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/](https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/)   
4. Multi-agent setup in Claude Code: non-specialist Claude to sequence implementation plan; Briefer serves as a conversation partner to discuss each increment step; Drafter produces initial code to be reviewed, refactored, and acceptance-tested; Critic observes the increment and provides feedback for the material. For consistency and to avoid re-setup costs, the instructions are stored in the repo-level CLAUDE.md file.
